title: GitHub - herdrdev/herdr-app: herdr desktop app · GitHub
content:
Herdr
Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.
Install
Linux and macOS
curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh
Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source. Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.
The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin. Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app. For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications.
Windows
Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):
irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex
Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.
Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.
Find your work
A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs. Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.
An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.
The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as:
Working: still busy.
Blocked: waiting for you.
Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere.
Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.
Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine.
The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.
Work on another machine
Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.
Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.
Make it yours
Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.
Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.
Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format.
Layouts and mods · Commands
Updates and privacy
Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves.
Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod.
For agents
herdr-app --skill
This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.
herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands
The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments.
Build from source
For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing.
Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI. Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git
cd herdr-app
just build
just test
just install
Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.
Documentation checks also need Bun: just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages.
To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:
python scripts/bench.py --bin <app executable> --set spinners --seconds 20
The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.
python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py.

title: GitHub - SheepSeb/tinyworldformer: Tiny world model generates games and stream ac plays them all on Pico 2W · GitHub
content:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action.
Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network.
Why
I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream.
Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout
The world model and the actor
network 1: the world model network 2: the actor
job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action
architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32
size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters
cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds
trained on recorded real games (how) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream (how)
The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough.
On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display.
The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself.
The games
Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/. It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap.
game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops
Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99%
Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below)
Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100%
Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45%
Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4%
"Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream).
You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout, doomlite, flappy, pong).
How the world model works
Frames split into tokens
The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector.
Looped Transformer
The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops.
The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right.
Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules:
Exact held-out frames by loop count:
loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man
1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6%
2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4%
3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7%
4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4%
Decoding
The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong):
Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently.
Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them.
Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted.
We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%.
Checking the world model
Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame (games/<game>.py: read), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward.
5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent (training/evalwm.py --agent):
game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step
Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) –
Doom-lite 1 0 1.50
Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00
Pong 1 0 0.00
Pac-Man 742 38 0.39
Training
First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game.
Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on (QAT).
The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico.
An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything.
The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it:
Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.
A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away.
Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as World Models (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found.
The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it (train --noise 0.3, as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite.
d=32 couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and d=48 could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed d=64.
The agents: stream-x
The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm.
The input is a feature vector read off the frame (training/streamx.py: observe_*, mirrored in Rust in tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is.
Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes.
Breakout
Doom-lite
Flappy Bird
Pac-Man lite
Pong
Greedy return in the real game, mean of 10 episodes, at snapshots of the same run:
game 0 1k 2k 5k 10k 20k 50k 100k 150k 250k 500k max
Breakout 8.2 17.0 15.9 21.9 29.9 29.9 29.9 31.1 35.0 39.9 45.6 56
Doom-lite −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 −5.0 59.5 69.9 78.1 81.8 82.1 82.9 –
Flappy Bird −1.0 −1.0 −1.0 1.9 24.6 24.9 96.2 123.7 309.2 332 332 332
Pac-Man 7.0 3.8 17.0 17.7 8.2 46.8 72.9 138.9 146.6 190.3 217.4 249
Pong −4.3 −3.9 −3.9 −3.9 −1.7 −2.0 −0.3 1.1 1.7 1.1 1.1 5
Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them. --idle-penalty 0.1 costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20 steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent patrols and gets twice the kills.
tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs is the same algorithm in no_std Rust, with the backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+ after 250k.
Quantization and the Pico
Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row (scale = max|w| / 127). Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges. Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per SMLAD instruction on the RP2350) and then apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU.
Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that was trained. rustexport/intref.py is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and cargo test checks golden vectors for every exported env.
game int8 weights float32 (embeddings, norms, scales) game data agent (float32) firmware flash firmware RAM
Breakout 19.7 KB 31.6 KB 1.1 KB 54.1 KB 361 KB 299 KB
Doom-lite 33.9 KB 91.9 KB 12.0 KB 61.3 KB 471 KB 357 KB
Flappy Bird 30.1 KB 69.5 KB 10.1 KB 50.8 KB 409 KB 227 KB
Pong 30.1 KB 70.4 KB 10.9 KB 52.6 KB 414 KB 244 KB
Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF (size -A), built with the Display Pack driver, so they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520 KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be int8 too.
src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other projects can reuse the export: build a model from rustexport.qat (QLinear, LoopedBlock), train it with ActQuant.enabled = True after a float warm-up, convert it with rustexport.convert.looped_model, then write the Rust source with int_model_arrays, mlp_arrays and codegen.write_module. rustexport.Golden writes the vectors a Rust test checks.
On the chip
The firmware (tinyworldformer-rs/firmware) is no_std Rust on embassy. Nothing is allocated at run time: the weights are static arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size static in RAM.
Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop (dream_loop in firmware/src/main.rs) is one frame:
The actor reads features off the current frame (agent::observe) and runs its MLP to pick a button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press is used.
The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button (Engine::forward), and decoding turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head; lives and episode ends are counters on top.
If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it.
The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen.
When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent runs as fast as the chip allows.
Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional Display Pack (--features display) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count.
Where the memory goes:
in flash in RAM
world model int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB) scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read, and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose per-cell scores alone take 184 KB)
actor float32 MLP weights and featur

title: H.264 is magic: a technical walkthrough of a remarkable technology.
content:
H.264 is Magic
Sid Bala
02 Nov 2016 • 10 min read
Share
H.264 is a video compression codec standard. It is ubiquitous - internet video, Blu-ray, phones, security cameras, drones, everything. Everything uses H.264 now.
H.264 is a remarkable piece of technology. It is the result of 30+ years of work with one single goal: To reduce the bandwidth required for transmission of full-motion video.
Technically, it is very interesting. This post will give insight into some of the details at a high level - I hope to not bore you too much with the intricacies. Also note that many of the concepts explained here apply to video compression in general, and not just H.264.
Why even compress anything?
A simple uncompressed video file will contain an array of 2D buffers containing pixel data for each frame. So it's a 3D (2 spatial dimensions and 1 temporal) array of bytes. Each pixel takes 3 bytes to store - one byte each for the three primary colors (red, green and blue).
1080p @ 60 Hz = 1920x1080x60x3 => ~370 MB/sec of raw data.
This is next to impossible to deal with. A 50GB Blu-ray disk will only hold ~2 mins. You can't move it anywhere fast. Even SSDs have trouble dumping this straight from RAM to Disk[^1].
So yeah. We need compression.
Why H.264 compression?
Yes, I will answer this. But first let me show you something. Here is the Apple Homepage:
I captured the screen of this home page and produced two files:
PNG screenshot of the Apple homepage 1015KB
5 Second 60fps H.264 video of the same Apple homepage 175KB
Eh. What? Those file sizes look switched.
No, they're right. The H.264 video, 300 frames long is 175KB. A single frame of that video in PNG is 1015KB.
It looks like we're storing 300 times the amount of data in the video. But the file size is a fifth. So H.264 would seem to be 1500x as efficient as PNG.
How is this even possible? All right, what's the trick?
There are very many tricks! H.264 uses all the tricks you can think of (and tons you can't think of). Let's go through the important ones.
Shedding weight
Imagine you're building a car for street racing. You need to go faster. What is the first thing you do? You shed some weight. Your car weighs 3000 lbs. You throw away stuff you don't need. Those back seats? pfft. Chuck those. That subwoofer? Gone. No music for you. Air Conditioning? Yeah, ditch it. Transmission? Ye..no. Wait! We're gonna need that.
You remove everything except the things that matter.
This concept of throwing away bits you don't need to save space is called lossy compression. H.264 is a lossy codec - it throws away less important bits and only keeps the important bits.
PNG is a lossless codec. It means that nothing is thrown away. Bit for bit, the original source image can be recovered from a PNG encoded image.
Important bits? How does the algorithm know what bits in my frame are important?
There are few obvious ways to trim out images. Maybe the top right quadrant is useless all the time. So maybe we can zero out those pixels and discard that quadrant. We would use only 3/4th of the space we need. ~2200 lbs now. Or maybe we can crop out a thick border around the edges of the frame, the important stuff is in the middle anyway. Yes, you could do these. But H.264 doesn't do this.
What does H.264 actually do?
H.264, like other lossy image algorithms, discards detail information. Here is a close-up of the original compared with the image post-discard.
See how the compressed one does not show the holes in the speaker grills in the MacBook Pro? If you don't zoom in, you would even notice the difference. The image on the right weighs in at 7% the size of the original - and we haven't even compressed the image in the traditional sense. Imagine your car weighed just 200 lbs!
7% wow! How do you discard detail information like that?
For this we need a quick math lesson.
Information Entropy
Now we're getting to the juicy bits! Ha puns! If you took an information theory class, you might remember information entropy. Information entropy is the number of bits required to represent some information. Note that it is not simply the size of some dataset. It is minimum number of bits that must be used to represent all the information contained in a dataset.
For example, if your dataset is the result of a single coin toss, you need 1 bit of entropy. If you have record two coin tosses, you'll need 2 bits. Makes sense?
Suppose you have some strange coin - you've tossed it 10 times, and every time it lands on heads. How would you describe this information to someone? You wouldn't say HHHHHHHHH. You would just say "10 tosses, all heads" - bam! You've just compressed some data! Easy. I saved you hours of mindfuck lectures. This is obviously an oversimplification, but you've transformed some data into another shorter representation of the same information. You've reduced data redundancy. The information entropy in this dataset has not changed - you've just converted between representations. This type of encoder is called an entropy encoder - it's a general-purpose lossless encoder that works for any type of data.
Frequency Domain
Now that you understand information entropy, let's move on to transformations of data. You can represent data in some fundamental units. If you use binary, you have 0 and 1. If you use hex, you have 16 characters. You can easily transform between the two systems. They are essentially equivalent. So far so good? Ok!
Now, some imagination! Imagine you can transform any dataset that varies over space(or time) - something like the brightness value of an image, into a different coordinate space. So instead of x-y coordinates, let's say we have frequency coordinates. freqX and freqY are the axes now. This is called a frequency domain representation. There is another mindfuck mathematical theorem[^2] that states that you can do this for any data and you can achieve a perfect lossless transformation as long as freqX and freqY are high enough.
Okay, but what the freq are freqX and freqY?
freqX and freqY are some other set of basis units. Just like when we switch from binary to hex, we have a different fundamental unit, we're switching from the familiar X-Y to freqX and freqY. Hex 'A' looks different from binary '1010'. Both mean the same thing, but look different. So here is what our image looks like in the frequency domain:
The fine grill on that MacBook pro has a high information content in the higher frequency components of that image. Finely varying content = high frequency components. Any sort of gradual variation in the color and brightness - such as gradients are low frequency components of that image. Anything in between falls in between. So fine details = high freq. Gentle gradients = low freq. Makes sense?
In the frequency domain representation, the low frequency components are near the center of that image. The higher frequency components are towards of the edges of the image.
Okay. Kinda makes sense. But why do all this?
Because now, you can take that frequency domain image and then mask out the edges - discard information which will contain the information with high frequency components. Now if you convert back to your regular x-y coordinates, you'll find that the resulting image looks similar to the original but has lost some of the fine details. But now, the image only occupies a fraction of the space. By controlling how big your mask is, you can now tune precisely how detailed you want your output images to be.
Here is the close-up of the laptop in the home page again. Except now, there is a circular border mask that's been applied.
The numbers represent the information entropy of that image as a fraction of the original. Even at 2%, you won't notice the difference unless you're at this zoom level. 2%! - your car now weighs 60 lbs!
So that's how you shed weight. This process in lossy compression is called quantization[^3].
Okay. Impressive, I guess. What else you got?
Chroma Subsampling.
The human/eye brain system is not very good at resolving finer details in color. It can detect minor variations in brightness very easily but not color. So there must be some way to discard color information to shed even more weight.
In a TV signal, R+G+B color data gets transformed to Y+Cb+Cr. The Y is the luminance (essentially black and white brightness) and the Cb and Cr are the chrominance (color) components. RGB and YCbCr are equivalent in terms of information entropy.
Why unnecessarily complicate? RGB not good enough for you?
Back before we had color TV, we only had the Y signal. And when color TVs just started coming along, engineers had to figure out a way to transmit RGB color along with Y. Instead of using two separate data streams, they wisely decided to encode the color information into Cb and Cr and transmit that along with the Y information. That way, BW TVs would only look at the Y component. Color TVs will, in addition, look at the chrominance components and convert to RGB internally.
But check out the trick: the Y component gets encoded at full resolution. The C components only at a quarter resolution. Since the eye/brain is terrible at detecting color variations, you can get away with this. By doing this, you reduce total bandwidth by one half, with very little visual difference. Half! Your car now weighs 30 lbs!
This process of discarding some of the color information is called Chroma Subsampling[^4]. While not specific to H.264 and has been around for decades itself, it is used almost universally.
Those are the big weight shedders for lossy compression. Our frames are now tiny - since we discarded most of the detail information and half of the color information.
Wait. That's it? Can we do something more?
Yes. Weight shedding is only the first step. So far we're only looking at the spatial domains within a single frame. Now it's time to explore temporal compression - where we look at a group of frames across time.
Motion compensation
H.264 is a motion compensation compression standard.
Motion compensation? What now?
Imagine you're watching a tennis match. The camera is fixed at a certain angle. The only thing moving is the ball back and forth. How would you encode this information? You do what you always do, right? You have a 3D array of pixels, two dimensions in space and one in time. Right?
Nah. Why would you? Most of the image is the same anyway. The court, the net, the crowds, all are static. The only real action is the ball moving. What if you could just have one static image of everything in the background, and then one moving image of just the ball? Wouldn't that save a lot of space? You see where I am going with this? Get it? See where I am going? Motion estimation?
Lame jokes aside, this is exactly what H.264 does. H.264 splits up the image into macro-blocks - typically 16x16 pixel blocks that it will use for motion estimation. It encodes one static image - typically called an I-frame(Intra frame). This is a full frame - containing all the bits it required to construct that frame. And then subsequent frames are either P-frames(predicted) or B-frames(bi-directionally predicted). P-frames are frames that will encode a motion vector for each of the macro-blocks from the previous frame. So a P-frame has to be constructed by the decoder based on previous frames. It starts with the last I-frame in the video stream and then walks through every subsequent frame - adding up the motion vector deltas as it goes along until it arrives at the current frame.
B-frames are even more interesting, where the prediction happens bi-directionally, both from past frames and from future frames. So you can imagine now why that Apple home page video is so well compressed. Because it's really just three I-frames in which the macro blocks are being panned around.
Let's say you've been playing a video on YouTube. You missed the last few seconds of dialog, so you scrub back a few seconds. Have you noticed that it doesn't instantly start playing from that timecode you just selected. It pauses for a few moments and then plays. It's already buffered those frames from the network, since you just played it, so why that pause?
Yeah that annoys the shit out of me. Why does it do that?
Because you've asked the decoder to jump to some arbitrary frame, the decoder has to redo all the calculations - starting from the nearest I-frames and adding up the motion vector deltas to the frame you're on - and this is computationally expensive, and hence the brief pause. Hopefully you'll be less annoyed now, knowing it's actually doing hard work and not just sitting around just to annoy you.
Since you're only encoding motion vectors deltas, this technique is extremely space-efficient for any video with motion, at the cost of some computation.
Now we've covered both spatial and temporal compression! So far we have a shitton of space saved in Quantization. Chroma subsampling further halved the space required. On top of that, we have motion compensation that stores only 3 actual frames for the ~300 that we had in that video.
Looks pretty good to me. Now what?
Now we wrap up and seal the deal. We use a traditional lossless entropy encoder. Because why not? Let's just slap that on there for good measure.
Entropy Coder
The I-frames, after the lossy steps, contain redundant information. The motion vectors for each of the macro blocks in the P and B-frames - there are entire groups of them with the same values - since several macro blocks move by the same amount when the image pans in our test video.
An entropy encoder will take care of this redundancy. And since it is a general purpose lossless encoder, we don't have to worry about what tradeoffs it's making. We can recover all the data that goes in.
And, we're done! At the core of it, this is how video compression codecs like H.264 work. These are its tricks.
Ok great! But I am curious to know how much our car weighs now.
The original video was captured at an odd resolution of 1232x1154. If we apply the math here, we get:
5 secs @ 60 fps = 1232x1154x60x3x5 => 1.2 GB
Compressed video => 175 KB
If we apply the same ratio to our 3000 lb car, we get 0.4 lbs as the final weight. 6.5 ounces!
Yeah. It's magic!
Obviously, I am massively oversimplifying several decades of intense research in this field. If you want to know more, the Wikipedia Page is pretty descriptive.
Have comments? Did I get something wrong? Not a fan of the lame jokes? Offended by the swearing? Use HackerNews or Reddit for voicing your opinion!
Or hit me up on Twitter or LinkedIn if you want to chat.
[^1]SSD Benchmarks
[^2]Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem
[^3][Quantization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantization_(signal_processing)
[^4]Chroma Subsampling

title: LLM Voice
content:
LLM Voice
29 October 2026
Martin Fowler
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion
There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.
I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)
Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves.
Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.
In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?
Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.
A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.
There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3. Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.
Notes
1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up.
2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source).
3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.”
Acknowledgements
Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post.
I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

title: GitHub - mottopanikeiku/doomformer: Compile an integer neural network into a DOOM map. Voodoo dolls do the arithmetic, light levels and plane heights hold the values, and every value is checked against NumPy with tolerance 0. · GitHub
content:
Doomformer compiles integer neural networks into ZDoom maps and runs them in ViZDoom. Voodoo dolls (the copies of the player that DOOM spawns for extra player-1 starts) do the arithmetic, and sector light levels and plane heights hold the sums. Python reads every exposed value back from the running game and compares it with a NumPy integer reference, tolerance 0. One value off by one and the run fails. It is slow: about 23,000 times slower than NumPy on a small MLP (engine time; 65,000 times with a timer around the whole call), and a handwritten digit takes 163 seconds of real-time DOOM in one map at the default schedule and 8 seconds at --opt 3.
Install · Proof · How it works · Films · Docs
Install and run
pip install git+https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer   # Python 3.11+, Linux or macOS
doomformer hello             # 2 s: a small MLP, every value checked
doomformer draw --digit 7    # 15 s: the marine walks a 7 and the level reads it
doomformer doctor checks ViZDoom, Freedoom and the display, builds ACC if it is absent, and compiles an ACS probe before reporting success. The first build needs git, cmake, a C compiler and network access to github.com. Linux uses dynamic runtimes: glibc-static is not required. On Fedora: sudo dnf install git cmake gcc gcc-c++ make. The Colab notebook needs no setup, but you draw on a browser canvas and doomformer mnist --image feeds it to DOOM, with no marine.
Proof: walk a digit, DOOM reads it
Holding FIRE, the marine inks a 3×3 brush of floor cells under him. READ makes the level write the 784 pixels into the network, and 1,355 voodoo dolls in the same map compute it. With --digit, Python stands in for you: it presses the marine's keys and USE once, then only advances the clock and reads.
          ▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄
       ▄████████████████
       ████▀▀     ▀████▀
       ▀▀▀        ▄███▀
                  ████
                  ███
                  ███
                  ███
                 ████
                 ███▀
                 ████
                 ▀███

DOOM reads: 7  (right)   -- the winner's doll lit it on the 7-segment display
EXACT: all 248 values DOOM computed [...] equal the NumPy integer reference (tolerance 0)
READ pass: 273 game tics = 8 s of real-time DOOM at 35 tics/s, 3 s wall [...]
Abridged at [...]; docs/commands.md has the whole output. draw builds its map with --opt 3, so a READ takes 273 game tics; at --opt 0, the original schedule, it takes 5,705 (163 s of real-time DOOM). Without --digit the command opens a window and you walk and draw yourself; DOOM then runs in real time.
The dolls compute 784 pixels → 64 hidden units → 45 pairwise score comparisons → 10 win counts. Only the digit that wins all nine of its comparisons gets a doll through, and the line that doll crosses starts the level script that lights the digit on the display. Python reads back the 784 pixels, the hidden layer, every comparison and the answer and checks all 248 values (119 values, each read with its negated twin, plus 10 outputs).
EXACT means DOOM equals the integer network. It says nothing about whether the digit is right. On the first 100 MNIST test digits DOOM reads 99 correctly, and 966 of 1,000 sampled from all 10,000; every result is exact. The integer network scores 97.16 % on all 10,000 (the float model scores 97.58 %). The 30 walked digits (0 to 9, three scripted stroke variants each) all read correctly and exact at --opt 3, and the network is also trained on that stroke distribution: the first version of this demo, a 784-32-10 network trained on MNIST alone, reads only 41.08 % of such strokes. Through real X key events a drawn 7 read exact at the default --opt 3; a 7 and a 1 were tried at --opt 0 with an earlier network. Details · film
The museum map: light a digit, rewire one connection
doomformer museum build writes museum.wad, a map you can play without Python. You step on seven floor pads to light a digit and press READ. 136 voodoo dolls compute a small hand-written network: each digit's score counts the segments that agree with it, and the winner's doll lights the display. MUTATE rewires one connection of that network inside the running level: segment a to digit 7 goes from +1 to -1, by changing the specials of its two weight lines. The same 7 then reads as 1, and RESTORE puts it back. The HUD and a scoreboard show the ten scores after each READ, and a camera station shows digit 7's sixth score doll: it passes its gate before MUTATE and stops in front of it after.
$ doomformer museum verify
7                        pads abc     w_7a +1  DOOM reads 7  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])
7 after MUTATE           pads abc     w_7a -1  DOOM reads 1  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])
7 after RESTORE          pads abc     w_7a +1  DOOM reads 7  scores [4, 6, 3, 5, 4, 3, 2, 7, 3, 4]  EXACT (148 values; 744 tics; [...])
Here Python plays: it presses the marine's keys and USE, and during each READ it only reads, with guarded readouts. It compares all 148 values with the NumPy reference of the network as it is wired at that moment. Without running DOOM, the static extractor also shows that the rewired map's netlist is the network with exactly that one weight changed. I have run the whole map only in ViZDoom. Its self-test map reads the digits 0 to 9, then the 7 after MUTATE and after RESTORE, without a player. On a GitHub runner it logs the exact values in GZDoom 4.14.2, LZDoom 3.88b, UZDoom 5.0.3 and ZDoom 2.8.1, and in Zandronum 3.2.1 only when every sector tag is below 32,768. Details
What is checked
Python reads sector light levels and floor and ceiling heights from the running game and compares each with an independent NumPy integer implementation of the same network. The check is integer equality over the runs that were made, and says nothing about inputs that were not run. The tests attack it: raising one weight line in a small compiled map from 5 to 6 must fail by exactly +1 on exactly the inputs whose dolls cross that line, and a readout that echoes a value Python wrote must fail (pytest tests/test_tamper.py, three tests, about 15 s).
Readback is guarded by default: before each page, Python poisons and checks its USER slots, then requires the page to replace them. Dropping a page cannot silently reuse a repeated input's answer or the previous page's values. guard=False is an explicit one-map historical opt-out. Guarded builds have new hashes (ACS and metadata, not geometry or arithmetic); the hash record explains the change.
doomformer fuzz --nets 40 compares every value of 40 random nets run in DOOM (306 passes, 0 mismatches, about 10 s with --workers 2; a planted compiler bug is found). fuzz --edge puts weights, biases and inputs at the range limits: 15,000 nets over ten fresh seeds, at --opt 0, at --opt 3 and as tile maps, made 113,605 passes and compared 1,987,632 values with no mismatch (the range check refused 47,686 of the inputs it drew, about 30 %), 3,000 more with the generator widened to plane starts near the bounds below (22,682 passes) and 2,000 more that also draw starts from 15,000 to 16,000 (14,782 passes), all with no mismatch. Earlier campaigns ran 2,000 random MLPs (15,374 passes, 276,594 values), 300 spiking nets and 100 random transformers over all 8 attention, norm and MLP variants (99 ran; one all-zero matrix is unsupported), after the scheduling fixes; 200 spiking --edge nets made 12,794 passes with no mismatch. fuzz --edge does not draw transformers. CI fuzzes 60 nets with a fresh, printed seed on every push and a longer campaign every Monday. The fuzzer and independent runs found four faults in this repo's own maps: two scheduling bugs and two plane limits. A plane move that starts more than 14,018 units from zero keeps its mover busy for three tics and drops the next request on that plane, and a plane that starts above 16,000 is exact on the first pass and wrong on later ones, so DOOM disagreed with the reference on nets that net.check had accepted. check and compile now refuse them: planes start inside [-15,000, 16,000] and move within ±14,018 (doomformer verify --plane-sweep, docs/verification.md).
doomformer verify runs every input class of a small MLP (the classes agree with every input on 20 of 20 nets, under an assumption stated in the same page). df.coverage counts what is compared: on MNIST all 248 exposed values, which are 129 values the reference defines and 119 twins, and the count falls when a readout name is dropped. The map does not expose the 903 staircase counts and 1,351 gate comparisons of the same net; they are checked through the sums they feed. doomformer verify --extract net.wad --net net.npz reads the net back out of a compiled map without starting DOOM and compares every weight, bias and threshold with the source net: the shipped MNIST net (784-64-45-10-10) comes back equal from its map alone at --opt 0 to 3, and so do 484 of 490 random nets at --opt 0 (the other 6 are equal but break the plane contract) and 199 of 199 at each of --opt 1 to 3. EQUAL covers the arithmetic netlist, the plane contract, the trigger and repeat flags, the mover speeds, the reset script and the readout pages; timing and geometry are printed as NOT CHECKED. A changed weight line shows as exactly that weight. Of 23,622 single edits to a small map at --opt 0 the extractor detects 17,906, and the 98 undetected edits that were run in DOOM on 12 inputs were all exact. It shows what the map says; that DOOM runs the map as read is what the exactness checks test. A mutation harness changes one line of a compiled map: of the 1,004 sites run (of 5,578) 297 are killed, all weight, sign and target classes among them. Of the 707 survivors 590 match a rule (a redundant scroller, a freeze line a forward pass never needs) that aggregate controls support, and 117 are input gaps (walking floors that only some inputs expose); none is proven equivalent. doomformer lint --fuzz compared the static schedule checker with DOOM on 5,397 maps: 0 false negatives. The method is translation validation (Pnueli, Siegel and Singerman, 1998): a test of each compile, not a proof that the compiler is right.
Who does what:
The dolls do every multiply-add, activation and comparison. ACS level scripts address cells, move input gates, rewind the dolls, sense the world and copy results out. None of the network's arithmetic runs in ACS. The toolkit's df.Agent is the one exception: it takes its argmax in ACS (docs/agents.md).
mnist: Python writes the 784 pixel ports and decides when the dolls have stopped; the dolls pick the digit.
demo and ask: Python writes the token ids and decides when the dolls have stopped, samples each letter from the logits DOOM computed and, when a model is cut into several maps, copies integers from one game to the next. demo --one-map is one map with no Python between layers; Python writes the tokens and samples the letter after each pass.
draw and his brain is the level: Python only advances the clock and runs readout scripts (in draw, from READ on). The level supplies the inputs (the 784 pixels, the sensed tokens) and the dolls pick the digit or the action.
demo --one-map --loop: Python only advances the clock and runs readout scripts. The dolls pick each letter and write it into the next position.
The fly loop: Python only advances the clock and runs readout scripts, after calibrating the step period on a separate game that it does write. The level draws the input spikes and the output spikes fire the thrust lines.
--opt 3 (the default of draw; elsewhere --opt 0, the original schedule with guarded readback): an ACS script copies each layer's light levels into the next layer's gate heights. It adds and compares nothing, and the dolls still do the sums, thresholds, comparisons and the choice, but "no ACS between layers" holds at --opt 0 to 2 only.
doomformer machine: the dolls run the program counter and the registers. By default the loop, the rewind and the halt check are an ACS script, and a stored program is loaded by the host before the first tic. With --clock dolls a loop doll and line specials restart, rewind and stop the level, and ACS only reads values and checks that the dolls have stopped (docs/machine.md).
learn digits: Python writes the pixels and the label of each example, advances the clock and reads; the dolls compute the scores, the argmax and the weight update (docs/learning.md).
python -m demos.brainlevel --lesion-at N or --lesion-when near|ahead: the level's own clock closes the doors of the lesioned units before decision N, or the first time the tokens it senses satisfy the condition; Python only reads.
In the draw, his brain, loop, fly and machine runs a wrapper (ReadoutOnly) makes any other call raise, and the commands are counted: 58 in a headless draw pass, 710 in the film run of his brain, 154 in the lesion run, 0 others.
The maps use ZDoom's UDMF format and ACS, so they need ZDoom (here ViZDoom 1.3.2 with Freedoom assets), not the 1993 executable. net.quantization_report(x) measures how far an integer model is from the float model it came from. EXACT does not.
How it works
docs/HOW_IT_WORKS.md maps each part of a network to a part of the map: a value to a group of dolls, a weight to a line, an activation to a staircase, attention to a corridor of ceiling gates, ablation to a door.

A matrix multiply. Each doll is one unit of an activation, and each lava line it crosses adds a weight.
Attention. Dolls squeeze under ceiling gates that another live value has lowered. Counting who gets through is a multiply.
The engine has sharp edges and the compiler works around them. A plane mover refuses a second request on the same plane for as long as the first is still moving, and the later one is lost. A teleport line cancels the lines a doll crossed earlier in that tic. A thing more than 32,767 units from a BSP node can be filed under the wrong sector, so every map fits 32,000 units. These are ZDoom 2.8.1 behaviours measured in ViZDoom 1.3.2. The 32,000-unit rule is needed on Linux; on macOS arm64 the wrap did not occur in the probe maps (cause not investigated), and the rule is kept everywhere. The exported probe maps and the hello brain also ran in stock ZDoom 2.8.1 (53 of 53 rows match), Zandronum 3.2.1 (50 of 53: it cannot find sector tags above 32,767) and GZDoom 4.14.2, LZDoom and UZDoom (44 of 53: planes are doubles there and the UDMF parser refuses coordinates beyond ±32,768; the coordinate wrap stays). The hello brain's logged values equal the NumPy reference in ZDoom, GZDoom, LZDoom and UZDoom, and in Zandronum once its tags are moved below 32,768. The doll-clock counter machine (multiply 7 9, 464 steps, 235,567 tics) and a SUBLEQ add also ran in GZDoom, LZDoom and UZDoom with every step's pc and registers equal to the interpreter's log; ZDoom 2.8.1 and Zandronum (tags below 32,768) ran a 50-step multiply and the SUBLEQ add exactly, and sta

title: Akimoto | A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta) | Animation Studies Journal
content:
ARTICLE
A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta)
Author: Daisuke Akimoto
Keywords: animation, militarism, Miyazaki, nationalism, non-killing policy, war
How to Cite:
Akimoto, D., (2014) “A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta)”, Animation Studies Journal 9(1). doi: https://doi.org/10.64864/a85b8d7f-b345-4fd3-a0ff-4f1b600c9b97


Introduction
Historically, animated cartoons and movies have been used as ‘propaganda’ in war (Roffat 2011). Some animated films, however, contribute to conveying an anti-war pacifist point of view (Takai 2011). As such, the film Porco Rosso (1992) can be categorized as “anti-war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 144). Although Miyazaki has been attracted by seaplanes designed and manufactured during the period between the First World War and the Second World War (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72), this film conveys the important memory of war, especially the interwar era and the post-Cold War world. Indeed, in an interview just before the release of Porco Rosso, Miyazaki stated that the film is relevant to the Gulf War, and referred to the Yugoslav Wars as ethnic and nationalistic conflicts (Miyazaki 1996, p. 519; Miyazaki 2002, p. 95). In this context, the film forwards Miyazaki’s anti-war message. This paper examines Porco Rosso (Kurenai no Buta), which is based on 15 pages of Hikotei Jidai (The Golden Age of the Flying Boat), a comic created by Hayao Miyazaki and released in the animation journal, Model Graphics, No.14-16 in 1990 (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72). A synopsis of the comic story is literally “typed” at the beginning of Porco Rosso, as follows: “This motion picture is set over the Mediterranean Sea in an age when seaplanes ruled the waves. It tells a story of a valiant pig, who fought against flying pirates, for his pride, for his lover, and for his fortune. The name of the hero of our story is Crimson Pig.” Scholarship on this film has focused on issues of “war and peace,” especially in terms of the “non-war” (hisen) message (e.g. Okuda 2003). Similarly, Kazami et al (2002), among others, (Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provide some answers to the central question of the film: Why did Porco turn into a pig? The primary reason is that he was traumatized by the war. Building on Kazami et al’s work, this paper attributes the reason that Porco became a pig to the following three aspects: “man, the state and war” (Waltz, 1959). According Kenneth Waltz, theorist of international politics, the causes of war occur on three levels: individual, domestic, and international. Like Waltz, I argue here that Porco became a pig because he hates the following three factors: man (egoism), the state (nationalism) and war (militarism). Accordingly, my analysis of Porco Rosso is situated in the framework of peace research and international relations, such as non-killing philosophy, soft power/hard power, and conflict prevention/conflict resolution.
Methodology
In the field of animation studies, animation films by Studio Ghibli have been frequently analyzed as a case study. Ghibli animation films are “often considered as artistic productions, both entertaining and meaningful” (Gan 2009, p. 36). There are a large number of publications on the Studio Ghibli’s films, particularly those directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004), for instance, examined Miyazaki’s works in comparison with the animated cartoons of Osamu Tezuka, the creator of Astro Boy (1963). Miyazaki’s films also have been discussed compared with Disney animation. For instance, Kaori Yoshida (2011) offered a comparative analysis on Disney’s Pocahontas (1995) and Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke (1997) in terms of national identity. Moreover, some scholars (e.g. Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provided comprehensive thematic or structural analyses of Miyazaki’s films. However, earlier studies on Miyazaki animation, or Miyazaki-related animation films, do not necessarily focus on the issue of war and peace. Therefore, this paper offers an analysis of Miyazaki-related animation films in terms of war and peace (Table 1). Although the Miyazaki-related films in Table 1 do not directly deal with war themselves, all of them are related to war and peace to a certain extent. Hols: Prince of the Sun (1968) was released in the middle of the Vietnam War (1965-1975) and some combat scenes of the film represent the war. Miyazaki was involved as an animator in the creation of the film with director Isao Takahata, a friend and colleague. Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984) is a masterpiece, and the film reflects the international politics during the Cold War. The Giant Warrior (kyoshinhei) that caused an apocalyptic war, or the Seven Days of Fire, functions as a symbol of nuclear weaponry. The confrontation between Pejite and Tolmekia, the two powerful countries in the story can similarly be regarded as reflection of the Cold War bipolar structure (Akimoto 2014a). Laputa: Castle in the Sky (1986) was also created during the middle of the Cold War. The number of nuclear warheads in the world reached its peak in the mid-1980s, and the military technology of the legendary castle, Laputa, also symbolizes nuclear weapons. In this film, the word, “peace” is used only one time by Muska, who tries to conquer the world by taking possession of Laputa’s military technology. Obviously, this is a “political satire” by Miyazaki (Akimoto 2014b). Grave of the Fireflies (1988), a fictional film about a Japanese boy and his little sister at the end of the Pacific War (1941-1945), was not directed by Miyazaki but instead by Isao Takahata, another Studio Ghibli director (Akimoto 2014c), but reflects similar anti-war sentiment. In the post-Cold War context, Miyazaki produced Porco Rosso (1992) which depicts the interwar period (1919-1939) of the Adriatic Sea in conjunction with the Yugoslavian War (1991). Miyazaki contributed to the creation of Whisper of the Heart (1994) that has a passing reference to the Second World War (1939-1945). Princess Mononoke (1997) deals with Japanese civil war as well as confrontation between humans and animals. Howl’s Moving Castle (2004) and the latest film, The Wind Rises (2013) are related to the 2003 Iraq War, and the Asia Pacific War (1931-1945) (Akimoto 2014d; Akimoto 2014e). Thus, the films in which Miyazaki or Studio Ghibli is involved can be analyzed from a perspective of peace research (peace studies), an academic field which examines causes of war and conditions for peace. While ethical and legal issues need to be carefully taken into consideration when teaching Japanese animation (McLelland 2013), Studio Ghibli animation films can be useful as educational materials at the university level (Yonemura 2003, p. 10), particularly in the fields of both peace research and peace education. From the perspective of peace research, Porco Rosso makes a particularly rich case study, particularly because Miyazaki won the best feature film award in the 1993 Annecy International Animation Film Festival (Annecy.org 2013). Due to the award, which is one of the most internationally prestigious animation film festivals, the film was internationally acclaimed, and Miyazaki characterized as “Walt Disney Nippon” (Christin 1997, p. 184). Most reviews of and scholarship on Porco Rosso tend toward general analysis, lacking a specific focus on war and peace (e.g. Animage 1992, 2011; Kazami et al. 2002; Okuda 2003; Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008). Moreover, Miyazaki himself has made similar comments on his own work (Miyazaki 1996, 1997, 2013). Yet, none of the earlier studies of the film have investigated them from a perspective of peace research. In order to examine Porco Rosso, which conveys a similar anti-war message to The Wind Rises (Kaze Tachinu) (2013), which narrates Japan’s interwar period and war responsibility (Akimoto 2013a), this paper employs an interdisciplinary approach which combines peace research with animation studies. As an analytical method, this paper combines keyword analysis described above with sequence analysis of character’s lines as well as historical events. The sequence analysis is useful tool to examine timeline sequence (Abbott 1995) and it is applicable to film studies with a particular focus on character’s lines in historical context. Accordingly, the five main characters as well as historical background of this film need to be overviewed in this section. First, the hero of this film is a pig, Porco Rosso who flies in his crimson seaplane, SAVOIA S-21. As a bounty hunter, he cracks down on Aero Viking (Sky Pirates) in the Adriatic Sea after the First World War. He used to be a human (Marco Paggot) and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force, but he decided to leave the army after the war and cursed himself, turning into a pig. As I outline below, Porco was traumatized by his experiences in the war (Animage 2011, p. 35-37). Second, Madam Gina, a childhood friend of Porco and a madam of Hotel Adriano, is one of the two heroines of this film. In the film, it is said that pilots in the Mediterranean Sea tend to fall in love with her and visit Hotel Adriano for her song. She was married to three pilots who were all members of the Flying Club she organized as a child, but all of them died in the Great War, or in a flight accident. Gina is in secret love with Porco and vice versa (ibid, p. 54-57). Third, Fiyo Piccolo, the other heroine, is a 17-year old female mechanic and the granddaughter of Master Piccolo. She repairs Porco’s seaplane and develops an adolescent infatuation with him (ibid, 43-45). Fourth, Donald Curtis, an American pilot and Porco’s rival, is hired by Aero Viking to fight against Porco. He is a competent pilot and has an ambition to first become a Hollywood movie star, and then US President afterwards. Curtis falls in love with Gina at first sight and falls for Fiyo next (ibid, pp. 48-51). Fifth, the Mamma Aiutos, one of the largest Aero Vikings in the Adriatic Sea, steals and kidnaps for a living after the First World War (ibid, p. 63-65). This study examines the five character’s lines in the following historical context as demonstrated by Table 2 below. At a macro level, the chronology of the interwar period as the historical background for the film needs to be taken into consideration, as this background is crucial in understanding the content of this film. At a micro level, key scenes and main characters’ lines of the film will be examined. This is also imperative to comprehend the implications of the film for the issue of war and peace. The sequence of the nine most significant scenes in the film are as follows: 1) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos 2) Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” 3) Gina’s Life in War and Peace 4) Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War 5) Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane 6) The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” 7) Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” 8) The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? 9) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle The main characters’ dialogue in these nine sections accordingly constitute the primary source to be carefully investigated, in combination with my earlier argument, and relevant publications as secondary source in the context of the interwar period. The sequence analysis of the film and characters’ lines will be examined by using keywords in peace research and international politics.
Findings 1. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos
The film begins with a scene in which the main character, Porco Rosso (who seems to be enjoying his vacation – drinking wine and taking a nap at a beach), wakes up with a phone call for an emergency. He works as a contract combat fighter pilot in order to crack down on flying pirates and gangs, such as the Mamma Aiutos. Although he left the Italian Army, he works for peace and security of the Adriatic Sea in place of Mussolini’s National Fascist Party. Italy was one of the member states of Security Council on the League of Nations (1920-1946), but its collective security system did not function, and eventually could not prevent the occurrence of the Manchurian Incident (1931) and the Abyssinian Crisis, or the Second Italy-Ethiopian War (1935-1936). In this way, Porco’s work in the film can be seen as police operations, to maintain peace and safety during the time period. As I will discuss, the international system is more anarchic in this age, and the police and military forces of Italy were not necessarily efficient or functional, leading to the populace in the film making a contract with Porco to crack down on flying pirates. In the field of peace research, Glenn D. Paige (2009) examines “non-killing” as an analytical terminology. This paper, therefore, uses the term “non-killing” as a research keyword. In the first battle scene of this film, Porco demonstrates his “non-killing” policy. In order to make money, save hostages, and to keep peace on the Adriatic Sea, Porco decides to crack down on the Mamma Aiutos, but remains true to his “non-killing” principles. In the battle scene with the Mamma Aiutos, it comes to light that Porco has no intention to kill the gang. Instead, he tries to shoot their aircraft without causing serious damage to the pirates and hostages, and then demands that they should leave half the money and hostages in exchange for their lives. Although he calls a bluff saying: “Or I’ll kill all of you,” his policy is very clear early on in the film.
2. Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention”
Female characters in this film (Gina and Fiyo) were depicted as attractive and peaceful heroines. In terms of gender studies, Kuwabara (2007) sheds light on the concept of “feminism” and the meaning of the crimson color reflected in the movie. In an application of politics and international relations, Tomoko Shimizu (2004) analyzes Ghibli animation in terms of “soft power” in the post-Cold War era. The concept of “soft power” was proposed by Joseph Nye, a Harvard Professor and political scientist. As opposed to “hard power” which based on military power, “soft power” can be defined as “the ability to get what you want through attraction rather than coercion or payments. It arises from the attractiveness of a country’s culture, political ideas, and policies” (Nye 2004, p. x). In this framework, Japanese animation can be understood as Japanese “soft power,” which works to enhance Japan’s international image and attractiveness as national interest. For example, Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004) used the term “power of Japan animation” to contextualize the Japanese animation industry, which has lasted more than 85 years. Likewise, William Armour (2011) described Japanese animation and manga for learning Japanese language as “soft power pedagogy” (p. 125).
