Clean tables. One-second buckets reconstructed from each worker's ordered raw query timings and measured start/finish interval; latency uses continuous percentiles. Lines use a centered 9-second moving average; legend values are unsmoothed full-run results.
First, we’ll explain how we improved COUNT performance. In the second half, we’ll go beyond unfiltered BM25 and simple COUNT queries to test search queries with different filters and sort orders, where ParadeDB is up to 66 times faster. We’ll explain why and discuss what these differences mean when comparing benchmarks and choosing a search engine for your application.
But first, let’s dive into making COUNT faster!
These results use a one-off server-side benchmark. Read the methodology or view the benchmark harness.
Optimization 1: Segment Partitioning
Below is the simple query we started with: count the number of documents matching the term database.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM hn_items
WHERE text === 'database';
When profiling this query visibility checking accounted for over 80% of our page accesses. This makes sense because for every match, we need to fetch and decode its ctid value (which TIN can skip because its document index is ctid).
Data structure Share of page accesses
Visibility map + stored CTIDs 1382 (81%)
Everything else (postings, metadata, etc.) 325 (19%)
While looking at the query we realised that we could use a (to be announced) feature that we’ve been working on: segment partitioning.
ParadeDB and TIN both store data in a structure which is similar to an LSM tree. At a high level this means data is partitioned into immutable segments that are merged together when they reach a size threshold: smaller segments are combined when enough data accumulates to reach the next size tier. A simple naive merging strategy is oblivious to the data contained within the segment, so we can assume that each segment effectively contains a random sample of the dataset.
Our new segment partitioning and merge strategy, based on the Spooky LSM compaction paper, lets us split up segments by the values of one or more columns. We’ve been building this for the past few months and will share a technical deep dive soon (the benefits we’re seeing for Top K and joins are huge). For the purposes of this query, the useful part is that we can partition by ctid (Postgres’ internal row identifiers), which gives each segment a disjoint range of Postgres page numbers1:
Without partitioning (overlapping min/max page ranges):

Postgres pages:  0----------2999  0----------2999  0----------2999
                 [ Segment A ]    [ Segment B ]    [ Segment C ]

With partitioning (disjoint page ranges):

Postgres pages:  0-----------999  1000-------1999  2000-------2999
                 [ Segment A ]    [ Segment B ]    [ Segment C ]
Each segment already stores the minimum and maximum ctid. With this layout, we can check that range against the visibility map up front. If every page in the range is marked all-visible, we can skip visibility checking (and all the visibility-related page reads) for that entire segment altogether.
With pure size-tiered compaction, those ctid min/max ranges can span most of the table. A single updated page can defeat the shortcut for most segments. Partitioning by ctid confines that effect to the segment covering the affected pages, so that other segments can continue skipping per-row checks.
For our benchmark query, this brought visibility-related page accesses down from 1,382 to just 30.
Optimization 2: Inverting Our DocId Map
But what about the case when at least one page in a segment’s ctid range does need to be visibility checked? This becomes more likely the further we get from the last (auto)vacuum, and we don’t want a few modified pages to force ctid reads for every match.
The TIN blog explains that needing to convert DocIds to ctid values introduces overhead, and that’s true. But what it doesn’t mention is just how efficient a DocId to ctid map can be.
Our existing approach stores a ctid for every document and fetches it for every match. Counting n matches meant n ctid lookups:
  Doc ID:    0       1       2       3       4       5       6
  CTID:    (10,1)  (10,2)  (11,1)  (11,2)  (11,3)  (15,1)  (15,2)
A much more efficient representation is to essentially invert the map: a compressed column that maps a Postgres page numbers (i.e. first number in the ctid tuple) to the first DocId found on that page. This works because our segments are already sorted by ctid, guaranteeing that documents on the same page have consecutive DocIds.
After: document boundaries indexed by page

  Heap page:      10  11  12  13  14  15  end
  Starting DocId:  0   2   -   -   -   5    7

  Page 11 --> doc IDs [2, 5)
With this new format, we can check the visibility map up front, then look up document ranges only for pages that need checking:
  Page needing checks:   11
  DocIDs needing checks: [2, 5)
  Query matches:         [0, 3, 6]
                             |
                             v
                    Only do a CTID lookup for DocIds in 2, 5) -> Doc 3
For the single-term count query above, after updating 1,000 rows, this reduced buffer accesses from over 7,500 to just under 400: a 95% reduction.
Optimization 3: Bitmaps are Great for Common Terms
Tantivy uses BP128 encoding for its posting lists. BP128 means that the postings array is divided into 128-sized blocks, where each block is bitpacked and delta-encoded. These blocks also carry the score bounds that let the blockmax algorithm skip uncompetitive blocks during BM25 ranking.
When profiling we found that this representation works well for most terms, with the exception of very common terms that have dense posting lists. For these common terms, we found that intersecting or unioning large BP128 arrays incurred significant overhead, and that representing postings as bitmaps instead made those unions and intersections much cheaper.
Document IDs: [1, 3, 4, 7]

Bitmap: one bit per possible document ID

  Doc ID:   0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
  Bit:      0 1 0 1 1 0 0 1

BP128: store gaps between document IDs, then bitpack

  Doc IDs:     1     3     4     7
  Gaps:        1     2     1     3
  In binary:  01    10    01    11
              └── 2 bits per gap ──┘

A second block starts at the 129th posting.
To demonstrate the tradeoff between BP128 and bitmaps, consider two scenarios. First, imagine two rare terms that each match 10 out of a million documents. Intersecting their BP128-encoded arrays requires only a handful of comparisons, whereas scanning two equivalent bitmaps means processing a million bits each, most of which are zeroes (i.e. wasted work).
Next, imagine that the two terms are common, each matching ~500K out of a million documents. That means their arrays are ~500K entries each. In this case, bitmaps can be more efficient because bitwise AND/OR can process 64 documents at a time, versus walking the arrays one entry at a time.
We introduced a bitmap representation of postings for sufficiently dense terms matching more than 10% of the documents. This change alone halved p99 latency in our Wikipedia count benchmark.
Now for the Rest of Search
TIN is very fast at the query shapes it’s optimized for: Top K by BM25 and counts. ParadeDB aims to be an Elasticsearch alternative on Postgres, and from that perspective, BM25 and counts are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the queries we see running in production.
For instance, consider the following search queries over the Hacker News dataset:
1. Filtered count
How many posts contain the term "database" AND received more than 10 Hacker News points?
ParadeDB
TIN
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM hn_items
WHERE text ||| 'database'
  AND score > 10;
ParadeDB sustained 777 QPS versus TIN’s 78 QPS, a 10.0x throughput difference.

2. Filtered Top K by BM25 relevance

ParadeDB

SELECT id, text, "by", score, pdb.score(id) AS relevance

PlanetScale agrees that these queries matter. To quote their own blog post:
“A good text index in Postgres must support all of those things while also handling joins, complicated WHERE clauses across full-text and other column types.”
TIN isn’t very fast at these filtered and time-sorted queries yet. But because their Wikipedia and StackExchange workloads only contain a single indexed text column, they do not expose this gap. Real application tables are wider: search results are commonly filtered by metadata values or ordered by fields like timestamps or numeric values.
Which brings us to a broader point: the workload you pick often determines the story you tell. When we first introduced our benchmarker, we explained that we built a tool that could accommodate any workload. PlanetScale designed one where TIN excelled. We appreciated that it exposed blind spots in our BM25 and count performance and rigorously drove optimizations over those queries.
But even though ParadeDB is faster on the queries above, we do not believe it establishes a “fastest search engine,” on Postgres or otherwise. No single benchmark can, especially one designed by the same team building the product. That applies to ParadeDB’s Hacker News benchmark just as much as PlanetScale’s StackExchange and Wikipedia benchmarks.
The only way to find out what’s fastest for you (the reader) is to test your own queries on your own data. There are many search query shapes and our goal is to accelerate as many of these shapes as possible. If search with filters, sorting, or facets are frustratingly slow on your current database, try running them on ParadeDB.
Is There a Fundamental Architecture Difference?
TIN’s launch post attributed its performance advantage to its choice of document identifier. As we explained in Part I, we were skeptical. But we do think there exists a deeper, fundamental architecture difference that explains the gap on these more complex queries: how much of the query can be pushed down to the index.
TIN is explicitly a text-only index. Each index covers one text column, leaving non-text filters to Postgres and its other indexes. For the queries we ran where we filtered by a numeric value or sorted by time, TIN relies on B-tree indexes over those non-text columns. On the other hand, ParadeDB is able to index all of those columns together in one index.
That distinction matters for both filtering and sorting. For queries with both text and non-text filters, the TIN and B-tree indexes must independently produce all their matches before they are combined. This misses opportunities to avoid large amounts of work: the B-tree doesn’t know which documents match the text query, so it can collect millions of matches that the intersection will later discard. For other sort orders, such as sorting by time, TIN cannot coordinate text matching with time ordering. Postgres must order the matches outside the index rather than letting the search track the newest 10 matches as it goes.
Modern engines like ParadeDB (and Elasticsearch) solve this problem by storing text and metadata structures together, keyed by the same document identifier. That lets query execution coordinate text matching, filtering, and ordering as it goes, instead of materializing large independent candidate sets and combining them afterward. For a deeper dive, see How We Optimized Top K in Postgres.
The index definitions used for these runs make the difference clear. ParadeDB keeps the searchable text and the fields used for filtering and ordering in one index:
CREATE INDEX hn_items_idx
ON public.hn_items
USING paradedb (
  ((text)::pdb.unicode_words(
    'pnorms=true',
  )),
  score,
  "time"
)
WITH (partition_by=ctid, target_segment_count=4);
TIN indexes text separately and uses B-trees for the other fields:
CREATE INDEX hn_items_text_bm25_idx
ON public.hn_items
USING tin (text)
WITH (initial_segment_count='4');

CREATE INDEX hn_items_score
ON public.hn_items USING btree (score);

CREATE INDEX hn_items_time
ON public.hn_items USING btree

title: GitHub - johncassil/dontallow: Auto-dismiss the macOS 'Allow X to find devices on local networks?' prompt. Presses Don't Allow for you, zero CPU idle, survives reboots. · GitHub
content:
dontallow
Auto-dismisses the macOS prompt:
Allow "Google Chrome" to find devices on local networks? This will allow the app to discover, connect to, and collect data from devices on your networks.
It presses Don't Allow for you, within a fraction of a second, every time. Zero CPU while idle. Survives reboots. Two short Swift files, no dependencies.
Why this exists
macOS (Sequoia and later) shows this prompt the first time an app touches the local network. The decision is supposed to be remembered. For many apps it isn't, so the prompt comes back on every launch, often for apps you aren't even using:
Chromium browsers (Chrome, Brave, Edge, Island, Arc) copy their own app bundle into a random temp folder at launch so the code signature survives in-place updates. macOS keys the Local Network decision to that random path, so the next launch looks like a brand-new app. Your Privacy settings fill up with duplicate "Google Chrome.app" rows that no longer point at anything.
Apps with versioned install paths (anything that installs into .../versions/1.2.3/) get a new row per update.
Misattributed prompts. macOS pins the dialog on whichever app it decides is "responsible", so you'll see prompts for apps that aren't running.
Some apps do legitimately use this permission: Chromecast and AirPlay discovery in browsers and media players, LAN multiplayer in games, printer and scanner utilities. If you use one of those features, answer Allow for that app (dontallow pause 10m while you do), and it's remembered as long as the app's path is stable. If you never use them, you never need to be asked.
There is no supported way to prune the list, no MDM payload to pre-deny the permission, and tccutil reset doesn't cover it. So: a small agent that answers "no" for you.
Install
brew install johncassil/tap/dontallow   # or: make && make install
dontallow install
dontallow install writes a per-user launchd agent, starts it, opens System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility, and prints the exact path to add if macOS doesn't prompt you. Accessibility is the permission that lets it press the button. It waits for the grant and confirms when the agent is active. dontallow status repeats the instructions any time the grant is missing.
Use
Command What it does
dontallow status Agent state, pause state, allowlist, recent dismissals
dontallow pause [1h] Leave prompts alone for a while (30m, 2h, 1d, forever)
dontallow resume Dismiss again
dontallow rules Decode the system's Local Network rule store and show what each Privacy row really is, including orphans
dontallow uninstall Stop and remove the agent
dontallow run --dry-run Foreground, log what it would do, press nothing
Each dismissal posts a notification naming the app and the pause command, so you never have to remember how to turn it off. Mute the notification in System Settings if you'd rather not see it.
When an app really does need local network access
Three options, pick whichever fits:
dontallow pause 10m, then launch the app and click Allow yourself.
Add the app's name to ~/.config/dontallow/allowlist (one per line, case-insensitive substring). Prompts for it are never touched.
Flip the toggle in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network. A dismissed prompt records a deny, which you can reverse there.
Set ~/.config/dontallow/grace to a number of seconds if you want a window to click Allow before the agent does (default 0.25).
How it works
The prompt is a window owned by the system process UserNotificationCenter. dontallow registers an Accessibility observer for window creation on that process and sleeps until one fires. It reads the dialog text, confirms it's a local network prompt and not something else, checks pause and allowlist, and performs the Accessibility press action on the Don't Allow button. If the press is refused it falls back to a synthetic click at the button's location.
It never modifies system files, never disables protections, and never chooses Allow.
Managed Macs
Local Network cannot be pre-set by MDM, but Accessibility can. For a fleet: build once, sign with a Developer ID, ship the binary plus a PPPC (Privacy Preferences Policy Control) profile granting Accessibility to its code requirement, and run dontallow install per user. No manual Settings step.
After upgrading
macOS keys the Accessibility grant to the binary's code signature, and every build (including brew upgrade) produces a new one. After an upgrade run dontallow status. If it says the grant is missing, remove the dontallow row in Accessibility settings and add it back from the path it prints. The agent re-attaches on its own within ten seconds. A future release signed with a Developer ID will remove this step.
Tests
make test
Unit tests cover the pure logic (dialog text parsing, duration and pause parsing, allowlist matching, launchd plist generation, and the Local Network rule decoder against a fixture archive). They build with plain swiftc and need no Xcode or SwiftPM. The end-to-end path (a real prompt, a real press) can only be checked on a Mac with Accessibility granted; the manual recipe is in Tests/INTEGRATION.md.
Compatibility
Builds with Apple's Command Line Tools alone. Xcode is not required.
Apple Silicon and Intel: Homebrew compiles natively on each.
macOS 13 or later to build; the prompt itself only exists on macOS 15 Sequoia and later.
Tested so far: Intel, macOS 26.6. Reports from other versions welcome.
English-localized macOS only for now. The matcher keys on the dialog text and the "Don't Allow" button title; localized strings are planned.

title: Spain train crash: What we know after two trains crashed with dozens feared dead
content:
What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
9 hours ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Vicky Wong
Watch: What leaked audio reveals about Spain train crash
Two trains crashed south of the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday morning, on the high-speed line to Seville.
At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision, when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning have been declared in the country.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
Where and when did the crash happen?
The crash happened at 08:53 (07:53 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, according to an account given by the Spanish government.
The privately run Iryo train was stationary on the state-run Renfe train barrelled into the back of it at high speed. Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown".
The crash caused some carriages to fall down an embankment.
All train traffic on the line was stopped at stations along the route.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
What caused the crash?
Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer failure at about 08:30 on Wednesday morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre that decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
1vanta3 / X via Anadolu / Getty Images
Audio recordings obtained by Spanish media between train controllers working in Madrid for a rail infrastructure company in Adif in Madrid and the train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move at 08:36 even though another one ahead had stalled.
In one recording, the controller tells the driver of the Renfe train to disconnect and reconnect the LZB mechanism that monitors train speeds, and then resume the journey at normal speed.
"Disconnect and reconnect LZB. Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."
Young athlete and former minister among victims
Bloodied, dazed and angry - how passengers' rail journey turned to disaster
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
Under normal protocols, the driver would be expected to continue moving at a maximum of 40km/h according to their line of sight, and not at normal speed on a track designed for speeds of up to 200km/h.
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
In a second audio recording between the driver of the Iryo train in front and the control centre, the driver says the train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda". After some exchanges, the control centre operator tells the driver to "resume the journey" normally.
The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
How many passengers were on board?
EPA
Aerial footage shows the extent of the damage and the emergency response
More than 540 people were on board both trains.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
Julieta Gallego, a 24-year-old Spanish female long jumper, and former government minister Fátima Báñez, 59, were among those killed in the crash.
More than 100 people were treated for injuries, according to Spanish authorities, and by the next day 50 of them were still in hospital, 15 in a critical condition.
How have the authorities responded?
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
Opposition conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, whose People's Party leads most opinion polls ahead of 29 November elections, said it was not the day to talk about political responsibility, but insisted "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure".
Most Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday and suspended their election campaign.
However, Santiago Abascal of the far-right Vox refused to take part in what his party described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.
Europa Press via Getty Images
A huge emergency response is under way
Three days of official mourning began on Thursday.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response was under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan had cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
The Spanish Civil Guard set up bureaus in Madrid, Toledo, Seville and Córdoba to investigate reports of missing persons.
"The top priority is the identification of the missing persons and the taking of DNA samples to be able to locate their relatives," the civil guard wrote in a post on X.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

Sylphide OS
What is it ?

Sylphide OS
What is it ?
Sylphide OS is a general-purpose Operating system for computers made from microcontrollers (MCU).
Lacking MMU, those boards are usually not able to run a full-fledge modern operating system such as Linux.
Yet they are now powerful enough to provide an environment very similar to home computers as we knew them from the 80's.
Context
Retrocomputing is all the rage nowadays, but it can mean a lot of different things.
There are people "restoring old computers" (mostly for playing and collecting), typically telling you that emulators dont feel genuine enough for their old memories.
Others, die-hard electronic freaks, are interested in 'recreation' of old computers, either with modern components (cheap, easy to source), or on the contrary with era-exact chips for those who can afford them.
There are emulators of all kind, at different layers (pure-software, FPGA based, cycle-accurate or higher level, ...). You can even find online emulators for almost all platforms before 1990.
Some are developing software, usually games, using modern computers and software, but targeting old computers.
This project is about yet another way: computers using modern microcontollers. There are cheap and more and more common. And of course we expect more will be available.
Purpose
Traditionally, computers are based on powerful processors, with lot of peripherals, more importantly keyboard, screen and mouse, while microcontollers are a lot less powerful, packing a small core with very little RAM and lot of embedded style peripherals on the same chip. Things like UART, SPI, ADC, I2C, counters, timers, and so on.
But of course, as technology evolves, the difference got blurred, and we start to see microcontrollers that can handle "computer-like" system design. It's not so much about compute power (MCUs have been very powerful from some time already), but rather about being able to output to a standard display like VGA or HDMI, rather than nothing, SPI-based small LCD screens, or DSI. To a lesser extent, input can also be challenging, lot of MCUs just have no USB host capability, and when they do, only one port can be used. You want at least two for keyboard and mouse, and ideally a third one for usb key.
When you manage to get all of that, you still have a severely constrained environment (low ram, low colors if any). It really feels like early computers from 80's/90's, both as a user and as a programmer. This is exactly the kind of 'retrocomputing' I'm after.
Here, a "computer" is defined as having:
keyboard and mouse input, usually either ps/2 or USB
a standard display connector: VGA or HDMI
a real framebuffer: no 'on-the-fly' video signal generation
storage, usually microSD card, but USB keys can also do
Network (ethernet/wifi) is not required, but is a great feature to have.
As a summary, it's targeted to platforms between "development boards" (MCU without display/keyboard/mouse) and Single-board computer which are usually able to run Linux.
This is open hardware, the PCB is designed with KiCad, and source files for both software and hardware can be found on the (mercurial) repository at https://freehackers.org/electronics/sylphide-os.
It is developed by Thomas Capricelli.
It's called Sylphide OS because Sylphide Consulting is the name under which I work as a consultant.
Hardware
From the beginning, Sylphide OS was designed to run on different platforms. Here are the currently targets, each one has a dedicated page.
Olimex esp32-p4-pc, the flagship product: new, powerful
Barebone raspberry pi Pico 2, my own minimalist attempt at VGA+USB on a rp2350.
FabGL, an old classic with PS/2 input and VGA
There's an emulator that runs on the (linux) host, used for development.
I got some other targets in mind. If you know of readily hardware that could use such an OS, tell me about it. Or even better, start a port by yourself (but please contact me first).
Software
Nowadays, a PC operating system is a big bundle of different software (kernel, drivers, libraries, programs). But "back in the days", it was rather an integrated and self contained program, focused on the graphical interface. Drivers were few, because each computer manufacturer, or even each computer model had it's own dedicated operating system.
That's what I want to recreate here.
Under the hood, Sylphide OS uses FreeRTOS, a low-level kernel typically used on this kind of platform. It provides helpers for running tasks and some low-level routines.
On top of that, Sylphide OS adds:
drivers for mouse, keyboard, display, storage and network
graphical interface
programs
It aims to be versatile enough to be usable on very limited platforms (small framebuffer, monochrome display, tiny RAM), while still being able to use features for higher specs ones.
The code is mostly C (low-level, drivers, rendering library) and C++ (for the graphical interface). Some targets use assembler for drivers. C++ is used in a very limited form, using only features that would not bloat software. You really want to be very careful with such limited resources.
Current status
Keep in minde it's only 0.1.
The focus was on having a clean/stable framework and proper drivers for a few targets.
What you get:
kconfig-based configuration
Framework: different SDKs, different platforms, tooling
Low-level rendering: framebuffer, bitmaps, fonts
Three targets (+ emulator), with proper drivers
Graphical interface with desktop, menu, windows, windowmanager, desktop icons. You might recognize a famous look.
Information panel displaying hardware and software details and demonstrating the color capabilities.
What you don't have yet, but definitely planned:
storage (microsd, usb)
network (ethernet, wifi)
widgets (button, checkbox, modal dialog, ..)
external programs (loading an executable from sdcard and execute it)
Project layout
The most important directories and files are:
.
├── docs                        # (this) documentation
├── main                        # software
│   ├── main.c                  # entry point: init + event loop
│   ├── gfx_generic.c           # fall-back for low-level graphic rendering
│   ├── bitmaps
│   ├── fonts
│   ├── arch                    # platform-specific code
│   ├── gfx                     # low-level graphic rendering (one for each bit depth)
│   └── gui                     # window manager, menu, widgets, ...
└── tools                       # helpers
Get in touch
If you want to follow the project, subscribe to my blog.
For contacting me, use old-school IRC (instant messaging). I'm on channel #freehackers, on the libera network.
If you don't know IRC already, the easiest way is probably this web interface or this other one.
You can also send me a message through this form.
Contributing
If you want to help writing Sylphide OS, really the first thing you should do is contacting me.
You can use our gitlab to fork the repository: first create an account on https://freehackers.org/explore (top-right "sign in"). There are connectors to github, gitlab and atlassian.
In case of problem, contact me, don't be shy.

About Sixteen Colors:
Sixteen Colors is an online archive for ANSI and ASCII artpacks. The artform was originally intended for display on computer textmode consoles. It gained popularity in the early nineties with the rise of dial-up Bulletin Board Systems (BBS).

At one point artists started to group together and release their work in collections released monthly, these collection are called artpacks. Rivalry resulted in fierce competition between these artgroups which only boosted activity. ACiD and iCE are examples of early prominent groups.

The rise of the Internet in the late nineties started the decline of BBS's and thus also the need and interest for ANSI/ASCII art. And although the need has almost vanished, still today artists are producing artpacks in collectives. Sixteen Colors aims to collect these artpacks as an archive in the public interest.

Want to know more? A good starting point is THE ART OF WAREZ is a short-film about the origins and history of the ANSI art scene.

Summary
Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.
We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.
Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.
Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in coding and defensive cybersecurity. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.
Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.
Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI
Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.
Built for the Builders.
Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

Testing by Booz Allen demonstrated the success of the European Mistral Large 4 model against our internal benchmark for source code security analysis. The model was able to match vulnerability detection recall rates against other frontier cyber models with a compelling cost curve. And, Mistral's support for model customization and data-sovereign deployment also lets us tailor it for our mission needs and client environments with strict data-residency requirements. In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. 
We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.
Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral Forge. For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.
Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.
Built for Work.
Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. 

For finance-related work, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models.

The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.
Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque Postale
See it in Action
Cyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.
Agentic webdev: with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.
Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.
Built for Sovereignty.
As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create. 
With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on. 
Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral Forge, and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral Studio. Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently.

Developments such as Mistral Large 4 demonstrate how sovereign and open-weight AI models can expand the range of trusted solutions available to European organizations. We are encouraged by the progress being made and continue to explore how advanced AI can contribute to strengthening critical capabilities, including cybersecurity.

For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.
Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft

title: GitHub - da-luce/astroterm: A planetarium for your terminal! Explore stars, planets, constellations, and more, all rendered right in the command line—no telescope required. ✨🪐 · GitHub
content:
🌌 astroterm
astroterm is a terminal-based star map written in C. It displays the real-time positions of stars, planets, constellations, and more, all within your terminal—no telescope required! Configure sky views by date, time, and location with precise ASCII-rendered visuals. See usage for all supported options!
astroterm is constantly improving, and we'd love to hear your ideas! If you have a suggestion or find a bug, please open an issue and share your feedback. See CONTRIBUTING.md for guidelines on building, testing, and contributing to astroterm.
The night sky above Singapore on January 2, 2025
See usage on how to obtain this view
Table of Contents
🌌 astroterm
Features
Installation
Usage
Troubleshooting
Citations
Data Sources
Features
🔭 Highly Customizable: Choose any date, time, and location to explore past, present, or future celestial events
📐 Accurate Rendering: View the moon, stars, and planets with as much precision as terminal graphics allow
🌘 Moon Phases: Precise lunar phases in real-time
🌌 Constellation Figures: Detailed constellation shapes
⚡ Performance Optimized: Lightweight and fast ASCII rendering
Stars over Sydney, Australia on January 6, 2025
Installation
Several installation methods are provided based on your platform. If none of these fit your needs, you can always build from source. Refer to troubleshooting for help resolving any issues.
Arch Linux
You can install astroterm from the extra repository using pacman:
pacman -S astroterm
Fedora
You can install astroterm directly from the Fedora package repository on Fedora 40+.
sudo dnf install astroterm
Homebrew
You can install astroterm from Homebrew via:
brew install astroterm
Nix
You can try the package in a temporary environment with the following command:
nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command astroterm
Argument flags are added by wrapping the command in quotes. For example:
nix-shell -I nixpkgs=channel:nixpkgs-unstable -p astroterm --command "astroterm -u -c"
To make astroterm available from your $PATH, add it to your configuration.nix:
environment.systemPackages = with pkgs; [
  ...
  astroterm
]
Guix
You can install astroterm directly from the Guix main channel starting from this commit.
guix time-machine --commit=4b5f0408e66392ab745dc0f7830732217d88f17d -- shell astroterm
Or after guix pull:
guix shell astroterm -- astroterm --help  # to try
guix package --install astroterm          # add to current profile
Prebuilt Executable
Unix
Download the latest executable using wget
wget -O astroterm "https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-<os>-<arch>"
Replace <os> with the appropriate platform:
Linux: linux
macOS: darwin
Replace <arch> with the appropriate architecture:
Linux: x86_64 (arm64 support to come after Ubuntu arm64 runners are available)
Apple Silicon (M-series): aarch64
Intel-based Macs: x86_64
To view all supported combinations, see the Releases page.
Run the executable
chmod +x ./astroterm
./astroterm
Windows
Download the latest .exe file using PowerShell's Invoke-WebRequest:
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/releases/latest/download/astroterm-win-x86_64.exe" -OutFile "astroterm.exe"
Run the .exe
.\astroterm.exe
Building From Source
Usage
Options
The --help flag displays all supported options:
Usage: astroterm [OPTION]...

  -a, --latitude=<degrees>  Observer latitude [-90°, 90°] (default: 0.0)
  -o, --longitude=<degrees> Observer longitude [-180°, 180°] (default: 0.0)
  -d, --datetime=<yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ss>
                            Observation datetime in UTC
  -t, --threshold=<float>   Only render stars brighter than this magnitude
                            (default: 5.0)
  -l, --label-thresh=<float>
                            Label stars brighter than this magnitude (default:
                            0.25)
  -f, --fps=<int>           Frames per second (default: 24)
  -s, --speed=<float>       Animation speed multiplier (default: 1.0)
  -c, --color               Enable terminal colors
  -C, --constellations      Draw constellation stick figures. Note: a
                            constellation is only drawn if all stars in the
                            figure are over the threshold
  -g, --grid                Draw an azimuthal grid
  -u, --unicode             Use unicode characters
  -b, --braille             Use braille characters for constellation lines
                            (requires Unicode)
  -q, --quit-on-any         Quit on any keypress (default is to quit on 'q' or
                            'ESC' only)
  -m, --metadata            Display metadata
  -r, --aspect-ratio=<float>
                            Override the calculated terminal cell aspect ratio.
                            Use this if your projection is not 'square.' A value
                            around 2.0 works well for most cases
  -h, --help                Print this help message
  -B, --bash-completions    Print bash completions
  -i, --city=<city_name>    Use the latitude and longitude of the provided city.
                            If the name contains multiple words, enclose the
                            name in single or double quotes. For a list of
                            available cities, see:
                            https://github.com/da-luce/astroterm/blob/main/data/
                            cities.csv
  -v, --version             Display version info and exit
Shell Completions
To enable Tab completions in Bash, add the following line to your ~/.bashrc:
source <(astroterm --bash-completions)
Example 1
To achieve the "spinning globe" effect as shown in the README GIF, use the following flags:
astroterm --color --constellations --speed 10000 --fps 64 --city Singapore
or
astroterm -cC -s 10000 -f 64 -i Singapore
for short. In fact, any city around the equator will work. Locations closer to the poles will look different because the apparent motion of the stars is more circular around the celestial pole rather than sweeping across the sky.
Example 2
Say we wanted to view the sky at 5:00 AM (Eastern) on July 16, 1969—the morning of the Apollo 11 launch at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. We would run:
astroterm --latitude 28.573469 --longitude -80.651070 --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00
Finding the precise coordinates can be cumbersome, so we could also use the nearest major city to achieve a similar result:
astroterm --city Orlando --datetime 1969-7-16T8:00:00 -m
While we're still waiting for someone to invent time travel, we can cheat a little by using Stellarium to confirm that this aligns with reality.
If we then wanted to display constellations and add color, we would add --constellations --color as options.
If you simply want the current time, don't specify the --datetime option and astroterm will use the system time. For your current location, you will still have to specify the --lat and --long options, or provide the nearest city with the --city option.
For more options and help, run astroterm -h or astroterm --help.
Tip
Use a tool like LatLong to get your latitude and longitude.
Tip
Star magnitudes decrease as apparent brightness increases, i.e., to show more stars, increase the threshold.
Troubleshooting
Release Won't Download via Curl
For some reason, curl does not follow the latest release redirect. Use wget to download the latest release or hardcode the tag in the link using curl. Or, just download via the releases page.
Broken Unicode on Linux
If Unicode characters do not display correctly in the terminal, you may need to configure your system's locale to support Unicode.
Temporarily set the locale (add this to ~/.bashrc or equivalent to permanently enforce)
export LC_ALL="en_US.UTF-8"
export LC_CTYPE="en_US.UTF-8"
Install and configure locales (example for Ubuntu/Debian)
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y locales
sudo dpkg-reconfigure locales
During configuration, select en_US.UTF-8 as the default locale.
Citations
Many thanks to the following resources, which were invaluable to the development of this project.
Map Projections-A Working Manual by John P. Snyder
Wikipedia
Atractor
Jon Voisey's Blog: Following Kepler
Celestial Programming: Greg Miller's Astronomy Programming Page
Practical Astronomy with your Calculator by Peter Duffett-Smith
NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
Paul Schlyter's "How to compute planetary positions"
Dan Smith's "Meeus Solar Position Calculations"
Bryan Weber's "Orbital Mechanics Notes"
ASCOM
A Fast Bresenham Type Algorithm For Drawing Ellipses
Data Sources
Stars: Yale Bright Star Catalog
Star names: IAU Star Names
Constellation figures: Stellarium (Converted from Hipparchus to BSC5 indices using the HYG Database—see convert_constellations.py)
Cities: GeoNames (Filtered and condensed using filter_cities.py)
Planet orbital elements: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
Planet magnitudes: Computing Apparent Planetary Magnitudes for The Astronomical Almanac

title: GitHub - herdrdev/herdr-app: herdr desktop app · GitHub
content:
Herdr
Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.
Install
Linux and macOS
curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh
Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source. Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.
The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin. Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app. For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications.
Windows
Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):
irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex
Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.
Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.
Find your work
A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs. Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.
An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.
The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as:
Working: still busy.
Blocked: waiting for you.
Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere.
Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.
Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine.
The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.
Work on another machine
Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.
Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.
Make it yours
Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.
Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.
Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format.
Layouts and mods · Commands
Updates and privacy
Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves.
Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod.
For agents
herdr-app --skill
This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.
herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands
The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments.
Build from source
For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing.
Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI. Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git
cd herdr-app
just build
just test
just install
Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.
Documentation checks also need Bun: just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages.
To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:
python scripts/bench.py --bin <app executable> --set spinners --seconds 20
The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.
python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py.

title: Senior Operating Systems / Hypervisor Engineer at Wasmer | Y Combinator's Work at a Startup
content:
Home
Jobs
Learn
Resume Review
Log in
Sign up
Wasmer · S19
Senior Operating Systems / Hypervisor Engineer
The Operating System for Edge Computing
Location
Remote
Type
Full-time
Experience
3+ years
Visa
US citizenship/visa not required
Rust
Embedded Linux
Apply to this role
About the role
Company: Wasmer (https://wasmer.io)
Type: Full-time
Location: Remote (CET ± 2)
---
Build an operating system that runs everywhere
Most engineers spend their careers using operating systems. A few get to build one. This role is for the second group.
At Wasmer, we're building WASIX — an OS emulation layer that brings full POSIX semantics to WebAssembly: threads, processes, fork(), sockets, TTYs, signals, the works. It's the kind of problem where you're reading Linux kernel source in one tab and the WebAssembly spec in another, deciding how mmap should behave on a platform that was never designed to have one.
If that sentence made you lean in rather than close the tab, keep reading.
\
What you'll work on
WASIX itself — designing and implementing syscall semantics, process and threading models, virtual filesystems, and networking stacks on top of WebAssembly. Where Linux behavior and Wasm constraints collide, you'll be the one deciding what "correct" means.
The Wasmer runtime — the sandboxing, scheduling, and memory-management machinery that makes thousands of Wasm "processes" run safely and fast on a single host. Think hypervisor problems, at a different layer of the stack.
Making real software just work — porting and running battle-tested Unix software (curl, bash, PostgreSQL-class programs) unmodified on WASIX, and fixing everything that breaks along the way.
Open source - a good chunk of your work will ship publicly, in one of Wasmers open-source repositories
You're probably a fit if you
Have 5+ years of systems-level engineering experience, with real-world work on Linux internals, hypervisors (KVM, Xen, Firecracker, etc.), or comparable low-level runtimes — not just as a user, but as someone who has debugged, extended, or built them.
Have a genuine, self-driven interest in OS and hypervisor design — you have opinions about scheduler behavior, memory models, or syscall interfaces, and can defend them.
Have proven Rust experience, are fluent C and comfortable diving into large, unfamiliar codebases.
Know POSIX deeply: processes, signals, sockets, file descriptors, memory management — the stuff most people only meet through man pages.

title: Agents in Games · Labs
content:
Agents in Games
October 2026
Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch
Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).
We teamed up with Olam Labs, which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.
Minecraft
Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon.
We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.
github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness
Civ50
50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.
The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.
At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

title: GitHub - SheepSeb/tinyworldformer: Tiny world model generates games and stream ac plays them all on Pico 2W · GitHub
content:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action.
Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network.
Why
I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream.
Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout
The world model and the actor
network 1: the world model network 2: the actor
job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action
architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32
size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters
cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds
trained on recorded real games (how) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream (how)
The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough.
On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display.
The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself.
The games
Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/. It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap.
game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops
Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99%
Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below)
Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100%
Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45%
Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4%
"Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream).
You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout, doomlite, flappy, pong).
How the world model works
Frames split into tokens
The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector.
Looped Transformer
The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops.
The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right.
Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules:
Exact held-out frames by loop count:
loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man
1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6%
2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4%
3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7%
4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4%
Decoding
The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong):
Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently.
Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them.
Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted.
We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%.
Checking the world model
Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame (games/<game>.py: read), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward.
5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent (training/evalwm.py --agent):
game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step
Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) –
Doom-lite 1 0 1.50
Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00
Pong 1 0 0.00
Pac-Man 742 38 0.39
Training
First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game.
Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on (QAT).
The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico.
An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything.
The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it:
Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.
A Breakout agent in the dream got 154 points with 26 bricks left, because the world model didn't remove bricks from the corner when it were hit. Doom-lite agents learned to snipe from 5 cells away.
Agents trained only in the dream scored 210 there (the real maximum is 56) and 28 in the real game, as World Models (Ha & Schmidhuber) predicts. Each collect-and-fine-tune round closed the exploit that agent had found.
The Doom-lite dream sometimes lost the enemy sprite and never drew it again: the model copied the previous view instead of redrawing it from the minimap. Noise augmentation fixed it (train --noise 0.3, as in GameNGen): input views get random pixels and sometimes lose the sprite.
d=32 couldn't absorb the wider Breakout data and d=48 could. Pac-Man's 48×48 frame needed d=64.
The agents: stream-x
The agents use Stream AC(λ) (Elsayed, Vasan & Mahmood, 2024), which learns from one transition at a time: no replay buffer, no batches, no target network. Eligibility traces carry credit back in time, and ObGD shrinks any step that would overshoot the TD target. The policy and value networks each have two hidden layers of 64 units (32 on the Pico) with LayerNorm.
The input is a feature vector read off the frame (training/streamx.py: observe_*, mirrored in Rust in tinyworldformer-rs/src/agent.rs). For example, the ball's row, column and heading in Breakout, or in Pac-Man, for each direction, the shortest-path distance to the nearest pellet and how close each ghost is.
Below is one training run per game (real game, 500k steps) at six stages: untrained, the end, and the snapshots where the score has covered 25, 50, 75 and 95% of the way. Each panel plays greedily from the same start and skips a few steps per frame. "try" counts the episodes played so far, so you can see the crashes.

Pac-Man 7.0 3.8 17.0 17.7 8.2 46.8 72.9 138.9 146.6 190.3 217.4 249
Pong −4.3 −3.9 −3.9 −3.9 −1.7 −2.0 −0.3 1.1 1.7 1.1 1.1 5
Without shaping, Doom-lite agents camp in the start corner and fire, because the enemy always comes to them. --idle-penalty 0.1 costs 0.1 for each step spent in a cell visited more than 6 times in the last 20 steps. The position is read off the minimap, so the penalty works inside the dream too. With it the agent patrols and gets twice the kills.
tinyworldformer-rs/src/learner.rs is the same algorithm in no_std Rust, with the backward pass written by hand. It matches 200 PyTorch updates to within 3.5e-6. On the host, a fresh agent inside the Rust int8 Flappy Bird dream averages 6 pipes per episode after 25k steps, 121 after 100k, and 300+ after 250k.
Quantization and the Pico
Every matrix in the world model is int8 with one scale per output row (scale = max|w| / 127). Activations are int8 too, with one scale per tensor and per loop index, since the loops see different ranges. Matmuls sum int8 × int8 into int32 (two multiply-adds per SMLAD instruction on the RP2350) and then apply one float multiply by the two scales. Softmax uses a 1024-entry exp table, with probabilities stored as uint8. Norms, residuals and embeddings stay in float32, since the RP2350 has an FPU.
Training applies the same rounding (QAT with a straight-through estimator), so the int8 model is the model that was trained. rustexport/intref.py is the int8 model in numpy with every float operation in a fixed order; the Rust engine reproduces it bit for bit, and cargo test checks golden vectors for every exported env.
game int8 weights float32 (embeddings, norms, scales) game data agent (float32) firmware flash firmware RAM
Breakout 19.7 KB 31.6 KB 1.1 KB 54.1 KB 361 KB 299 KB
Doom-lite 33.9 KB 91.9 KB 12.0 KB 61.3 KB 471 KB 357 KB
Flappy Bird 30.1 KB 69.5 KB 10.1 KB 50.8 KB 409 KB 227 KB
Pong 30.1 KB 70.4 KB 10.9 KB 52.6 KB 414 KB 244 KB
Flash and RAM are measured from the firmware ELF (size -A), built with the Display Pack driver, so they include the code, USB, the display driver and the on-device learner. The Pico 2 W has 4 MB of flash and 520 KB of SRAM, 512 KiB of it in the main memory map. The float32 embedding tables are the largest part and could be int8 too.
src/tinyworldformer/rustexport/ imports only numpy and torch (a test keeps it that way), so other projects can reuse the export: build a model from rustexport.qat (QLinear, LoopedBlock), train it with ActQuant.enabled = True after a float warm-up, convert it with rustexport.convert.looped_model, then write the Rust source with int_model_arrays, mlp_arrays and codegen.write_module. rustexport.Golden writes the vectors a Rust test checks.
On the chip
The firmware (tinyworldformer-rs/firmware) is no_std Rust on embassy. Nothing is allocated at run time: the weights are static arrays in flash, and every buffer is a fixed-size static in RAM.
Core 1 runs the game. One pass of its loop (dream_loop in firmware/src/main.rs) is one frame:
The actor reads features off the current frame (agent::observe) and runs its MLP to pick a button. If on-device learning is on, the learning agent picks instead; if you are pressing buttons, your press is used.
The int8 transformer runs 2 loops over the frame and the button (Engine::forward), and decoding turns its scores into the next frame: background argmax per cell, each singleton placed once (sampled for random events with an xorshift RNG), then the sprite stamps. The reward is the argmax of the reward head; lives and episode ends are counters on top.
If learning is on, the learner updates from this one transition and then forgets it.
The frame goes to core 0 through a two-slot channel. If core 0 is still busy with the previous frame, this one is dropped, so core 1 never waits for the screen.
When you play, core 1 slows down to a playable speed (66–150 ms per frame, depending on the game). The agent runs as fast as the chip allows.
Core 0 runs embassy async tasks for everything else. Over USB serial, each frame goes out as coloured ANSI text with a status line (model time, actor time, fps, env and agent names), and keys come back in. The optional Display Pack (--features display) is a 320×240 ST7789 over SPI at up to 62.5 MHz, and only cells that changed since the last frame are redrawn. Its buttons are polled every 20 ms. The two cores share only the frame channel and a few atomics: who is playing, the pressed key, learning on/off, and the loop count.
Where the memory goes:
in flash in RAM
world model int8 matrices, float32 embeddings, norms and scales, the game's opening frames and colours (52–138 KB) scratch buffers for one forward pass: activations for 36–80 tokens, the int8 copies the matmuls read, and the per-cell scores of the next frame (114 KB for Flappy Bird up to 368 KB for Pac-Man, whose per-cell scores alone take 184 KB)
